Cognitive Decline and Dementia in an Adult

tempo · first domain lost · companion signsOver years, stepwise, or weeks to months, and what came with it?

1Presentation2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Presentation
Bottom line
  • Dementia: decline in memory or thinking with intact consciousness that costs independence in daily activities. First exclude delirium and depression
  • Every new decline: CBC, metabolic panel, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and vitamin B12, HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) and syphilis testing by risk; brain MRI if the cause is still unclear, to exclude a structural cause
  • Tempo and companions name the cause: memory loss over years (Alzheimer), stepwise (vascular), fluctuation, visual hallucinations, dream enactment (dementia with Lewy bodies, or Lewy body dementia), weeks to months with startle myoclonus (Creutzfeldt-Jakob)
What it is

Acquired decline in memory or thinking, with intact consciousness, enough to need help with daily activities

Who

Older adults; Alzheimer disease is the most common cause, vascular dementia the second

Sort by

Tempo: years, stepwise, or weeks to months first domain lost: memory, executive or visuospatial function, or personality companions: parkinsonism, gait and incontinence, myoclonus, alcohol use

Treatment in

2Urgent risks
Acute changeSudden confusion in a patient with known dementia

If attention and alertness wax and wane, choose look for infection, pain, a metabolic derangement or a medication effect.

Alcohol or malnutritionAlcohol use or malnutrition with confusion, ataxia or eye-movement abnormalities

If Wernicke encephalopathy is possible, choose thiamine; glucose without thiamine can precipitate Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

HallucinationsVisual hallucinations in suspected dementia with Lewy bodies (Lewy body dementia)

If the hallucinations need treatment, choose avoid typical antipsychotics such as haloperidol; a cholinesterase inhibitor is first-line; if psychosis is severe or distressing, low-dose quetiapine may be used with extreme caution.

Rapid declineDementia progressing over weeks to months

If startle myoclonus or cerebellar signs appear, choose MRI, electroencephalogram (EEG), and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) 14-3-3 protein and real-time quaking-induced conversion (RT-QuIC) for prion disease.

3Differential
Causes, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintTimelineDecides it
Alzheimer diseaseShort-term memory lost first, then language and spatial disorientation; personality changes laterInsidious, over yearsMemory lost first; no focal deficits early; medial temporal (hippocampal) atrophy is the earliest imaging finding
Dementia with Lewy bodies (Lewy body dementia); see Fluctuating attention, early well-formed visual hallucinations, dream enactment, parkinsonism; executive and visuospatial loss before memoryDementia before or within 1 year of parkinsonism; dream enactment may come years earlierDementia plus 2 of 4 core features: fluctuation, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, REM (rapid eye movement) sleep behavior disorder
Delirium; see Waxing and waning attention and alertnessAcuteConsciousness altered; dementia leaves it intact
Depression-related cognitive impairment (pseudodementia); see Depressed mood; distressed by memory loss; often answers "I don't know"Acute onset with the depressive episodeAware and distressed, unlike dementia; does not explain parkinsonism, fluctuation or dream enactment
Vascular dementiaTypically early executive dysfunction, focal neurologic signs, vascular risk factorsStepwise declineInfarcts or white matter changes on imaging
Frontotemporal dementiaEarly disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, compulsive behavior such as hyperoralityOnset typically in the 40s or 50sMemory and visuospatial function relatively spared early; frontal and anterior temporal atrophy
Normal pressure hydrocephalusGait disturbance, urinary incontinence, slowed attention and apathy; a reversible cause MnemonicWet is urinary incontinence, wobbly is gait apraxia, wacky is dementiaGait problem earlyDilated ventricles; gait improves after lumbar puncture
Creutzfeldt-Jakob diseasePersonality change, sleep disturbance, startle myoclonus, cerebellar and upper motor neuron signs Sporadic or acquiredUsually sporadic, after age 50; rarely iatrogenic (neurosurgical instruments, corneal or dura grafts, growth hormone) or variant, from contaminated beefWeeks to months; fatal within about a yearPositive CSF RT-QuIC; cortical ribboning on MRI; periodic sharp waves on EEG
Korsakoff syndrome; see Alcohol use disorder; confabulation without concern; recent memory lost, remote memory kept; anterograde amnesia more prominent than retrogradeChronic; may follow a Wernicke episode or develop without oneAlert, with no ataxia or eye findings, unlike Wernicke encephalopathy; rarely recovers
Parkinson disease dementia; see Established parkinsonian motor diseaseDementia more than 1 year after motor onsetTiming of dementia against motor onset
Encephalitis (herpes simplex, autoimmune or paraneoplastic)Usually fever, headache, seizures and focal deficits (herpes); a tumor such as small cell lung cancer (paraneoplastic)Under 1 week (herpes)MRI, CSF and EEG separate it from prion disease
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Dream enactment, good and bad days, rigidityDementia with Lewy bodiesCholinesterase inhibitor; avoid haloperidol
Alcohol use disorder, confabulation, remote memory intact, unconcernedKorsakoff syndromeThiamine; memory rarely recovers
Startle myoclonus after months of declineCreutzfeldt-Jakob diseaseCSF RT-QuIC; supportive care, counseling and social services
Slow memory loss over years, no focal deficitsAlzheimer diseaseCholinesterase inhibitor such as donepezil; memantine is an option ExpectationsCholinesterase inhibitors improve cognitive function but do not alter the course
Stepwise decline with focal signs, typically with vascular risk factorsVascular dementiaMRI for infarcts
Early disinhibition or apathy with memory relatively sparedFrontotemporal dementiaMRI for frontal and anterior temporal atrophy
Gait problem, incontinence, enlarged ventriclesNormal pressure hydrocephalusLumbar puncture; shunt if gait improves
Depressed, aware of and distressed by memory lossDepression-related cognitive impairmentTreat the depression with an SSRI

Pause point. The bait: a head CT (often normal early in prion disease) or a nonspecific 14-3-3 read as the answer, or haloperidol for hallucinations in Lewy body dementia. Name the tempo and the companion signs first.

Practice
  1. 74-year-old man; his wife reports he punches and shouts while asleep Some mornings he seems himself; by afternoon he is confused. He recently got lost driving home Exam: symmetric rigidity, slow gait; recall is near normal → Dementia with Lewy bodies → Dream enactment, fluctuation and parkinsonism with early visuospatial loss and relatively spared memory fit Lewy body dementia; Alzheimer disease starts with memory loss, and Parkinson disease dementia follows motor disease by over a year
  2. 61-year-old man who drinks heavily is found entering a neighbor's house He gives a fluent, false reason and is unbothered by gaps in his story He recalls his school years in detail; gait and eye movements are normal → Korsakoff syndrome → Confabulation with lost recent memory, preserved remote memory and no concern, in alcohol use disorder, is Korsakoff syndrome; Wernicke encephalopathy brings confusion, ataxia and eye findings
  3. 58-year-old woman has declined over 3 months and can no longer dress herself A slammed door makes her arms jerk; she now sleeps most of the day Head CT is normal; routine CSF shows no white cells → CSF RT-QuIC → Rapid decline with startle myoclonus and sleep disturbance suggests Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease; a positive RT-QuIC confirms it, while CT is often normal and herpes encephalitis evolves within a week with fever
  4. 55-year-old man now sleeps 14 hours a day and drifts into the right lane when driving Over 2 months he developed a wide-based gait and dysmetria CSF RT-QuIC is positive; reflexes and sensation are normal → Myoclonus → A positive RT-QuIC confirms Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, in which startle myoclonus usually develops; prion disease affects upper motor neurons, so flaccid paralysis is not expected
  5. 70-year-old woman has 6 weeks of poor sleep, low appetite and slowed thinking She insists her memory is failing and often answers "I don't know" She is tearful and worried; no parkinsonism or focal deficits → Depression-related cognitive impairment → Acute onset with depressive symptoms and distress about memory point to depression-related cognitive impairment; patients with Alzheimer disease are typically relatively unconcerned
  6. 76-year-old man first developed an unsteady gait, then urinary accidents Over several months he became slow to answer and apathetic Brain MRI shows dilated ventricles; no infarcts or mass lesion → Lumbar puncture to remove CSF → Gait disturbance, incontinence and cognitive slowing with dilated ventricles suggest normal pressure hydrocephalus; gait improvement after lumbar puncture supports it, and a shunt is the definitive treatment
  7. 68-year-old man has forgotten appointments and repeated questions for a year He now needs help paying bills; his wife says he is alert and calm Exam shows no focal deficits; no recent medication changes → CBC, metabolic panel, TSH and B12 → A slow decline with intact alertness and lost independence is dementia; laboratory testing first excludes reversible contributors before a cause is named
  8. 80-year-old man with Lewy body dementia sees strangers in his room at night The visions frighten him; attention fluctuates and his limbs are rigid His family asks for medication to stop the hallucinations → Haloperidol → Typical antipsychotics such as haloperidol can markedly worsen rigidity, confusion and falls in Lewy body dementia; a cholinesterase inhibitor is first-line, and low-dose quetiapine is a cautious option for severe psychosis
Pairs with Delirium: an acute change on top of dementia. Parkinson Disease and Parkinsonism: Lewy body and Parkinson disease dementia. Substance Intoxication and Withdrawal: Wernicke encephalopathy. Major Depressive Disorder: depression-related cognitive impairment.
Transferable rule

Exclude delirium and depression before naming a dementia; then the tempo and the companion signs choose the cause.
